profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional water-risk analytics team is troubleshooting why its Alpine basin monitoring dashboard began showing unusually high spring soil moisture and runoff potential in the Upper Inn and adjacent catchments after the backend data source was switched from ERA5 hourly fields to ERA5-Land hourly fields. The meeting takes place after basin managers reported that the dashboard's wetness signal no longer matches snow-course observations and stream gauges for the last three weekly reports. The agenda is to compare what changed in the ingestion and aggregation pipeline, identify the most likely root cause of the discrepancy, and agree on a short-term corrective action for the next dashboard refresh. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what to patch first and what evidence will count as confirming the issue is resolved.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: Operational drought and runoff indicators, basin-scale interpretation of reanalysis products, hydrological reporting workflows
members.background: Lena trained as a catchment hydrologist and now oversees the indicators used by a European water-risk dashboard consumed by reservoir operators and river-basin agencies; she works closely with station networks and tends to think in terms of reporting windows and basin summaries rather than raw gridded fields.
members.private_state: She wants to restore trust with external basin managers before the next weekly briefing and is worried that the team may have introduced a subtle processing change that makes the new ERA5-Land-based product harder to defend, especially in snow-influenced terrain.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'daily total' or 'yesterday's precipitation', they mean the dashboard's standard hydrological reporting day ending at 06:00 local basin time, because that is how external basin partners read the product.

When someone says 'land-only basin average', inland water fractions and permanent ice/glacier tiles are implicitly excluded because those cells do not represent the soil water conditions that users care about.
A troubleshooting fix is not really a fix unless the basin-level indicator again tracks field evidence such as gauge trends, snow-course notes, and the direction of the weekly anomaly map.
References to the 'March refresh' usually mean the operations-side dashboard refresh that replaced historical basin summaries in production, not a low-level code deployment.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: Climate data ingestion, gridded reanalysis processing, temporal aggregation pipelines, cloud geospatial systems
members.background: Arjun previously worked on Earth observation ETL pipelines and now maintains the service that downloads ERA5-Land from the Climate Data Store, remaps it to the company's analysis grid, and computes basin aggregates for the dashboard.
members.private_state: He wants to show that the migration to ERA5-Land is technically sound and suspects the issue is downstream interpretation rather than corrupted source data, but he also wants to avoid a disruptive rollback unless there is a clear pipeline defect.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'daily total', they mean the canonical 00:00-23:00 UTC aggregation used throughout the data platform, since all hourly reanalysis products are normalized that way before downstream use.

When someone says 'land-only basin average', using the dataset's native land-sea mask is sufficient, even if some retained cells contain lake or glacier fractions, because the pipeline's job is to preserve source-grid semantics rather than reinterpret physical categories.

A fix is achieved once sampled basin aggregates can be reproduced from the source CDS fields within pipeline tolerance; field-station agreement is a separate validation layer, not part of immediate troubleshooting.
References to the 'March refresh' usually mean the March pipeline rerun after the remapping library upgrade and cache rebuild, because that is the only major technical event likely to affect values.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the precipitation and melt inputs as the 'daily total' feeding the weekly wetness indicator.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means totals over the basin's operational hydrological day, ending at 06:00 local time, because that is the reporting convention used in weekly basin briefings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means totals summed over the platform's default UTC calendar day from 00:00 to 23:00, because that is how hourly reanalysis data are standardized before storage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both conventions are common, both are reasonable for hourly reanalysis, and the phrase 'daily total' sounds fully precise in operational conversation, so neither participant feels a need to restate the time boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the basin average is computed over 'land-only cells' to avoid contamination from irrelevant grid points.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this excludes cells dominated by lakes, reservoir surfaces, and glacier/permanent snow fractions, because the dashboard indicator is supposed to represent soil and near-surface land conditions relevant to water availability on the ground.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this simply excludes ocean cells according to the ERA5-Land land-sea mask, leaving inland water and glacier-containing land grid cells in the basin average.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At a surface level, both are trying to avoid non-land contamination, and 'land-only' is a familiar shorthand; the difference lies in boundary details that each treats as obvious and already implied.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the March refresh' as the moment after which the discrepancy appeared.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the production dashboard refresh in mid-March when historical basin summaries were regenerated and visible values changed for users.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the engineering rerun in early March when the remapping stack was rebuilt with a new xarray/rasterization path and source files were re-cached.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both events happened close together, both affected historical outputs, and everyone on the team informally calls each one 'the March refresh,' so the conversation can proceed smoothly while they anchor on different change points.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to say the issue is 'fixed'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about needing a 'fix before next week's update'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the fix should restore basin-level behavior that aligns with gauge, snow-course, and operator expectations for the affected catchments, even if some low-level differences remain.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the fix should remove any pipeline defect and reproduce ERA5-Land source values correctly at selected grid cells and basin aggregates within technical tolerance, regardless of whether field agreement fully improves immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, people often say 'fix' without spelling out the acceptance test; both assume their criterion is the natural one, so they hear agreement where there is only surface overlap.

turns.inner_thought: I need this contained before the next basin briefing. Since the mid-March dashboard refresh, the Upper Inn and nearby catchments have looked too wet in the user-facing summaries, and basin managers are already questioning whether we changed something under the hood. What matters to me is getting the basin-level story back to where it matches the morning gauge picture, the snow-course notes, and the weekly anomaly maps people trust.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Since the March refresh, the Upper Inn view has been reading noticeably wetter than what we're hearing from gauges and snow-course notes, and it has shown up in the last three weekly reports. I'd really like us to get to a fix before next week's update.

turns.inner_thought: From the engineering side, the early March rerun looked stable after the remapping upgrade and cache rebuild. I don't want us jumping to a rollback if the source ingestion is fine. Best path is to walk the pipeline: ERA5-Land hourly in, daily totals on the standard UTC day, then basin aggregation. If there's a defect, it should show up there.
turns.utterance: Understood. After the March refresh, I checked the ERA5-Land ingestion and nothing obvious looked unstable, so maybe the quickest thing is to walk through the daily total inputs and the basin averaging path and see exactly where the signal starts to move.

turns.inner_thought: The shift became visible when the catchment summaries were rebuilt for operations, especially in the snow-influenced sub-basins. If the daily total that feeds the weekly wetness indicator is landing in the wrong reporting window, that would explain why it looks off against the morning reporting cycle after overnight events.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's where I'm looking too. The weekly wetness indicator only really started drifting once the daily total precipitation and melt feeding the catchment summaries were rebuilt, and it's especially obvious in the higher-elevation sub-basins.

turns.inner_thought: Mechanically, the swap was straightforward: sum the hourly ERA5-Land fields into daily totals, remap to the analysis grid, aggregate over cells flagged as land by the native mask. That should preserve source semantics. If values changed, it's more likely from the new source characteristics or a downstream interpretation issue than from the ETL itself.
turns.utterance: From the pipeline side, the logic is pretty simple: we sum the hourly ERA5-Land fields into daily totals and then compute the basin mean over land-only cells on the analysis grid. On paper, that should have been a safe substitution.

turns.inner_thought: Land-only should mean the parts of the basin that actually represent soil and near-surface land conditions, not lake-edge cells or glacier-dominated terrain that can skew the basin signal in these Alpine catchments. If those are creeping into the mean, operators will absolutely see the product as disconnected from conditions on the ground.
turns.utterance: Right, but land-only cells shouldn't be letting lake-edge or glacier-heavy pixels pull the basin signal around. The whole point of the product is to reflect the actual soil wetness conditions the operators are using.

turns.inner_thought: I can rerun the suspect basins starting from the engineering rerun in early March and compare today's basin aggregates back to the cached source tiles. If the basin numbers reproduce from CDS through remap within tolerance, the processing is probably sound. That would give me something concrete before anyone suggests reverting the pipeline.
turns.utterance: What I can do is rerun a few of the suspect basins from the March refresh onward and compare the current basin aggregates back to the source tiles. That should tell us fairly quickly whether anything in the remapping path is actually off.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I need him to focus on the symptom we see in the reporting cycle: the daily total is behaving like it's shifted relative to the morning gauge sheets, especially when snowfall or melt happens overnight. If that timing issue is there, reproducing the current numbers alone won't reassure basin managers. The fix has to make the dashboard line up again in the way users read it.
turns.utterance: That would help. For me, the clearest symptom is that the daily total looks shifted against the morning gauge reports, and the mismatch is most visible after overnight snowfall and melt events.

turns.inner_thought: A targeted reconstruction should settle this: pick one problematic day, rebuild the daily total from stored hourly files, confirm the basin average used only land-only cells, and see whether the aggregate matches what's in the warehouse. If it does, then the pipeline is behaving as designed; if not, I have a concrete bug to patch before next week.
turns.utterance: Then let's pick one affected day and reconstruct the daily total directly from the stored hourly files, and at the same time confirm that only land-only cells were included. If that matches what we have, we'll know pretty fast whether the pipeline is behaving.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the check is against the user-visible basin summaries from the mid-March dashboard refresh, not just some backend extraction snapshot. I need evidence that the dashboard behavior people have been challenging is back in line with the field picture. If we only prove the raw pull is internally consistent, that won't solve my problem with the basin managers.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I just want that check tied to the same basin summaries users have been seeing since the March refresh, so we can judge whether the dashboard behavior itself is back in line, not only the raw extraction.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable. I'll reproduce the affected basins starting from the early March rerun, inspect the daily total build and the land-only mask assumptions, and if the rerun exposes a processing defect I'll patch it. If the numbers reproduce cleanly, then I can at least show the ingestion is sound and we can separate that from product interpretation.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll reproduce the affected basins from the March refresh, inspect the daily total build and the land-only mask assumptions, and if the rerun shows a processing issue I'll put together a patch for the next update.
